newsitem.title: USA: Baby Bell sues to break down long-distance barriers.
newsitem.headline: Baby Bell sues to break down long-distance barriers.

text.p: Baby Bell phone company SBC Communications Inc. on Wednesday filed a federal lawsuit seeking access to the lucrative domestic long-distance market, a company lawyer said.

In the lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Wichita Falls, Texas, SBC challenged sections of the 1996 telecommunications act that opened local calling networks but banned regional Baby Bells from offering long-distance and other services to their local customers, attorney Jim Ellis said.
"The thrust of the suit is that singling out and discriminating against those (Baby Bell) companies violates several provisions of the U.S. Constitution," Ellis said.

San Antonio-based SBC also planned to appeal last week's Federal Communications Commission ruling blocking the company from offering long-distance service in Oklahoma, one of seven states where it operates local calling networks.

The appeal, which will be filed Thursday in the U.S. District Court of Appeals in Washington, is part of SBC's push to gain full access to the $80 billion-a-year domestic long-distance market and the lucrative international calling market, analysts said.

"We are asking the courts to let us compete just like GTE (Corp.) and all these other companies," he said. "If we are successful, sometime in the next three to six months we will be permitted to be in the long-distance business in our seven states."
In Washington, FCC Commissioner Susan Ness accused SBC of trying to circumvent Congress' intent to introduce local phone competition before allowing new entrants in the long-distance market.

"SBC's lawsuit appears to be an effort to circumvent that framework, to enable it to offer long-distance service without first opening its local markets to competition," Ness said in a statement referring to the Texas lawsuit.

The company in the lawsuit also contested provisions of the law blocking Baby Bells from offering security alarm monitoring services, publishing electronic yellow pages and manufacturing telecommunications equipment, Ellis said.

But the company is not challenging sections of the landmark law that ended monopoly control of local calling markets, opened the markets to rivals and required the Baby Bells to resell services, he said.

The Baby Bells have been barred from entering the national long-distance market since the 1984 breakup of AT&T, and face increased competition for their share of the $100 billion-a-year local-calling business.

The Baby Bell by the end of the year will seek regulatory approval to offer long-distance service in the seven states -- California, Texas, Oklahoma, Nevada, Arkansas, Kansas and Missouri -- where it offers local service.

SBC stepped up its push to enter the long-distance markets on equal footing with rival carriers after its reported talks on a $50 billion merger with long-distance giant AT&T Corp. broke down last week after coming under fire from regulators.

SBC's bid to offer long-distance service to its customers in Oklahoma was supported by state regulators but rejected jUNE 26 by the Federal Communications Commission, which said SBC had failed to adequately open its monopoly market in the state to competitors.

State regulators argued that allowing SBC into the long-distance market would force long-distance rivals like MCI Communications Corp., Sprint Corp. and AT&T to compete in the local calling market as customers sought one carrier to provide both services.

SBC contends its service territory has been opened to competitors -- including long-distance providers and cable television companies -- but said competition has failed to emerge because rivals have only offered service in metropolitan areas.
